extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of natural philosophy / evolutionary theory (19th-century educated audience)
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length philosophical exposition of the 'law of evolution' arguing what changes count as true evolution versus dissolution, illustrated across astronomy, geology, biology, society, language, and science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolution as change from the homogeneous to the heterogeneous
rubrics_metrics.description: "Evolution is a change from the homogeneous to the heterogeneous."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a defining characteristic: development exhibits a multiplication of unlike parts. Examples given include organic development (formation of distinct organs), social differentiation, and cosmical concentration. Note that mere increase of heterogeneity per se is not sufficient (see distinction with disease/death).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolution as change from the indefinite to the definite
rubrics_metrics.description: "At the same time that Evolution is a change from the homogeneous to the heterogeneous, it is a change from the indefinite to the definite."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definiteness means increased distinctness with which parts are marked off from one another — an advance from confusion to order, from undetermined arrangement to determined arrangement. This criterion distinguishes progressive multiformity from disorganizing multiformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish evolutionary heterogeneity from disorderly heterogeneity by increase in definiteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Heterogeneity that is accompanied by increased definiteness counts as Evolution; heterogeneity that destroys definiteness (is indeterminate) is not Evolution but Dissolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern examples: morbid growths, decomposition, social rebellion, famine — these may increase heterogeneity but produce indeterminate, confused arrangements rather than ordered distinctness. Use locality, extent, outline, internal structure, and proportion to judge definiteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Features of definiteness (what to look for in evolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definiteness is shown by precision in locality, extent, outline, constant proportions, and clear internal structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: normal organs have precise relative positions and constant proportions; embryological structures become more 'marked out with slowly-increasing precision.' In geology/planetary formation, shapes and force-relations become more sharply defined (e.g., oblate spheroid → more specific outline; planes of motion merge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Features of indefiniteness (anti-pattern indicators)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indefiniteness is shown by variable sizes, lack of constant proportions, vague margins, confused internal structure, and gradual blurring of organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: morbid growths (warts, cancers, tubercles) lack precise position and proportion; decomposition blurs minute structure; social disorder fuses ranks and obliterates prior lines of organization. Use these signs to judge when change is dissolution rather than development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-domain evidential requirement: find the indefinite→definite pattern across domains
rubrics_metrics.description: To support the law of Evolution one should observe the advance from indistinct/indefinite to distinct/definite structure in multiple domains: cosmical, geological, organic, specific (species), social, linguistic, scientific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter supplies domain-specific illustrations (nebular hypothesis and planet formation; cooling Earth and crust/continents; embryology and organogenesis; species divergence via natural selection; social organization from tribes to nations; languages gaining inflections and vocabulary; science moving from qualitative to quantitative). A convincing account seeks analogous definite-making processes across these domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embryological development as a test of definiteness-increase
rubrics_metrics.description: Embryology demonstrates stepwise transitions from vague cell-masses to distinct organs and systems (e.g., blastoderm → area germinativa → primitive trace → vertebral canal; heart and liver differentiation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stages of increasing precision (membrane formation, canalization, septa formation, ducts with clearly-marked walls) as empirical exemplars of the indefinite→definite criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species-level evolution criterion: divergence and elimination of intermediates
rubrics_metrics.description: If species have arisen by natural selection, there must be a tendency to divergence, with disappearance of intermediate forms so that contrasts between groups become greater.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a mechanism-consistent criterion: look for loss of intermediate varieties and formation of distinct and stable species (examples: races of men and domestic animals). Absence of such divergence weakens a natural-selection account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social/institutional evolution judged by increased specificity of roles, boundaries, and rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Societies evolve from wandering, indeterminate tribes to nations with settled territorial boundaries, distinct social classes, defined priesthoods, and precise institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical evidence (Egypt, Assyria, India, China, European constitutional development) showing sharper social divisions, fixed laws, and elaborated conventions as markers of definiteness. Apparent decreases in definiteness may indicate a social metamorphosis (transition between social types) rather than genuine devolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and science evolve toward greater definiteness (increase vocabulary, grammatical precision, and quantification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Languages gain inflections, additional parts of speech, multiplied terms, and fixed meanings; Science moves from qualitative associations to quantitative, exact relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators include larger vocabularies, lexical definitions (dictionaries), grammatical fixation, Euclidean arrangement of theorems, transition from empirical heuristics to formal methods (calculus, method of limits), and improved predictive accuracy (astronomical timing from days to seconds). These are empirical signs of the indefinite→definite trend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Over-definiteness / excessive fixation as a precursor to decline
rubrics_metrics.description: An increase of definiteness that continues after heterogeneity growth ceases may produce rigidity of structure, restricted function, narrowed variation, and ultimately decay/old age or institutional decline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: completion of epiphyses in bones and subsequent rigidity; organizations accumulating restrictive rules and precedents until they cannot adapt. Use caution: definiteness is good up to the point it permits necessary variation and adaptation.
